Q: Why is the current date being changed on the result set of cursor inside procedure? A:

As a hypothesis:
The DB2 date is represented as 4 bytes: 2 bytes is the year, 1 byte is the month, and 1 byte is the day.
In that order (YYYY-MM-DD)

I assume that you are getting the column value (most likely integer or possibly date) in the YYYYMMDD format. On your client side (where you show '2027-12-04') you are considering it in the YYYYDDMM format.

Next, convert something like

DATEFFROMPARTS(YYYY,DD,MM) 
instead of 
DATEFFROMPARTS(YYYY,MM,DD)

It is possible that such a default is accepted on your client side.
Further

'2026-04-28' ->DATEFFROMPARTS(2026,28,04)->(2026,12+12+04,04)->'2028-04-04'   
Or
'2026-04-29' ->(2026,12+12+5,4)-> '2028-05-04'

Or simpler examples

'2026-04-11' ->DATEFFROMPARTS(2026,11,04)->(2026,11,04)->'2026-11-04'  
'2026-04-12' ->DATEFFROMPARTS(2026,12,04)->(2026,12,04)->'2026-12-04'  
'2026-04-13' ->DATEFFROMPARTS(2026,12,04)+(13-12=1 montht)->(2027,01,04)->'2027-01-04'

This conversion will cause an error on some systems (SQL Server).
In some systems, it will be calculated as I have shown in the example (VBA) dateserial(2026,24,04) ->2027-12-04

"The query runs without any issues when executed on its own." -> issue is on client side, not DB2.

I suggest you look at what default date format settings you have installed on the client side.

Q: How to compare two csv files using a common index file by looping through each data column? A:

Data, after cleaning the samples:

index <- structure(list("Source column" = c("Handedness", "Handedness", "Handedness", "Drinking habits", "Drinking habits", "Drinking habits", "Drinking habits", "Drinking habits", "Smoking", "Smoking", "Smoking", "Smoking", "Smoking", "Exercise", "Exercise", "Exercise", "Exercise", "Exercise"), "Source code" = c("Left", "Right", "Ambidextrous", "Daily", "Weekly", "Monthly", "Yearly", "Never", "Daily", "Weekly", "Monthly", "Yearly", "Never", "Daily", "Weekly", "Monthly", "Yearly", "Never"), "Source value" = c(1,  2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 4, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6)), row.names = c(NA, -18L), class = "data.frame")
original <- structure(list(Vol_ID = c(8750L, 9526L, 4428L, 6134L, 7891L, 5280L, 9042L, 3176L, 6603L, 4819L), Handedness = c("Right", "Left", "Right", "Left", "Right", "Right", "Left", "Right", "Left", "Right"), "Drinking habits" = c("Daily", "Weekly", "Never", "Monthly", "Weekly", "Never", "Daily", "Weekly", "Weekly", "Never"), Smoking = c("Daily", "Daily", "Never", "Never", "Weekly", "Never", "Daily", "Never", "Weekly", "Daily"), Exercise = c("Weekly", "Never", "NA", "Weekly", "Daily", "Weekly", "Never", "Monthly",  "Weekly", "NA")), row.names = c(NA, -10L), class = "data.frame")
processed <- structure(list(Per_ID = c(8750L, 9526L, 4428L, 6134L, 7891L, 5280L, 9042L, 3176L, 6603L, 4819L), Handedness = c(2L, 1L, 2L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 2L, 1L, 2L), "Drinking habits" = c(1L, 2L, 0L, 3L, 2L, 0L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 0L), Smoking = c(1L, 1L, 0L, 0L, 3L, 0L, 1L, 0L, 2L, 1L), Exercise = c(2L, 6L, NA, 2L, 1L, 2L, 6L, 3L, 2L, NA)), row.names = c(NA, -10L), class = "data.frame")

A pipeline that pivots, joins, compares, and unpivots:

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr) # pivot_*
out <- pivot_longer(original, -Vol_ID) |>
  left_join(index, join_by(name == `Source column`, value == `Source code`)) |>
  left_join(pivot_longer(processed, -Per_ID), join_by(Vol_ID == Per_ID, name)) |>
  mutate(QC = case_when(`Source value` == value.y ~ "Match", is.na(`Source value`) ~ "No data", .default = "No Match!")) |>
  select(Vol_ID, name, value.x, QC) |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = Vol_ID, names_from = name, values_from = c(value.x, QC), names_glue = "{name}_{.value}") |>
  rename_with(.fn = ~ gsub("(_value|\\.x)", "", .x))

Here's the output with naive-sorting the columns:

select(out, Vol_ID, all_of(setdiff(sort(names(out)), "Vol_ID")))

#    Vol_ID `Drinking habits` `Drinking habits_QC` Exercise Exercise_QC Handedness Handedness_QC Smoking Smoking_QC

#  4   6134 Monthly           Match                Weekly   Match       Left       Match         Never   Match

Q: How can I set a placeholder (sentinel) without using None? A:

You should probably use a sentinel value. In Python 3.14 and earlier, this is typically (though not always!) done using a bare object combined with an identity (is) check:

import ast

SENTINEL = object()
user_input = SENTINEL
while user_input is SENTINEL:
    try:
        user_input = ast.literal_eval(input("Enter a Python literal: "))
    except:
        pass

The benefit of this pattern is that SENTINEL is completely unique. No other user-created object will ever compare identical to it. As such, there's no chance of collision with user-provided input; even another object() will not be identical to your sentinel. In fact, you can create multiple unique sentinels for different use cases:

SENTINEL_1 = object()
SENTINEL_2 = object()
assert SENTINEL_1 is not SENTINEL_2

Be careful to always use identity, not equality (==), when comparing to sentinels. Otherwise, someone could redefine __eq__ on the other object in an undesirable way:

SENTINEL = object()
class AlwaysEqual:
    def __eq__(self, other, /):
        return True
assert SENTINEL is not AlwaysEqual()
assert SENTINEL == AlwaysEqual() # Bad!

In Python 3.15, using an object like this will no longer be necessary. PEP 661 introduced a built-in sentinel class, which is very similar to the old pattern:

SENTINEL = sentinel("SENTINEL")
assert SENTINEL is not None
SENTINEL_2 = sentinel("SENTINEL_2")
assert SENTINEL is not SENTINEL_2

Like an object sentinel, new sentinels should always be compared with is and not ==.

It will also play nicely with type hints (though in this case, a bare None would also work):

SENTINEL = sentinel("SENTINEL")
five_characters: str | SENTINEL = SENTINEL

while five_characters is SENTINEL:
    user_input = input("Enter five characters: ")
    if len(user_input == 5):
        five_characters = user_input

Before 3.14, this wouldn't have worked; you generally would've needed to introduce more overhead such as using a class rather than an object as your sentinel value.

Q: How can you parse a string that is json from an existing temp table using PySpark? A:

From pyspark.sql.functions , you can use any of from_json, get_json_object, json_tuple to extract fields from json string as below,

>>from pyspark.sql.functions import json_tuple,from_json,get_json_object
>>> from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
>>> spark = SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()
>>> l = [(12, '{"status":"200"}'),(13,'{"status":"200","somecol":"300"}')]
>>> df = spark.createDataFrame(l,['pid','response'])
>>> df.show()
+---+--------------------+
|pid|            response|
+---+--------------------+
| 12|    {"status":"200"}|
| 13|{"status":"200",...|
+---+--------------------+

>>> df.printSchema()
root
 |-- pid: long (nullable = true)
 |-- response: string (nullable = true)

Using json_tuple :
>>> df.select('pid',json_tuple(df.response,'status','somecol')).show()
+---+---+----+
|pid| c0|  c1|
+---+---+----+
| 12|200|null|
| 13|200| 300|
+---+---+----+

Using from_json:
>>> schema = StructType([StructField("status", StringType()),StructField("somecol", StringType())])
>>> df.select('pid',from_json(df.response, schema).alias("json")).show()
+---+----------+
|pid|      json|
+---+----------+
| 12|[200,null]|
| 13| [200,300]|
+---+----------+

Using get_json_object:
>>> df.select('pid',get_json_object(df.response,'$.status').alias('status'),get_json_object(df.response,'$.somecol').alias('somecol')).show()
+---+------+-------+
|pid|status|somecol|
+---+------+-------+
| 12|   200|   null|
| 13|   200|    300|
+---+------+-------+

Q: TensorFlow cholesky decomposition A:

The Code :


@tf.function(jit_compile = True)
def f(S, jitter = 1e - 6)
    N = tf.shape(S)[-1]
    batch_shape = tf.shape(S)[:-2]
    I = tf.eye(N, batch_shape = batch_shape, dtype = S.dtype) 
    S_stab = S + jitter * I 
    L = tf.linalg.cholesky(S_stab)

    def solve(B): return tf.cholesky_solve(L,B)
return solve,L

Explanation :
If the Raw data tensor X has the shape [2, 3, 4, 4]
(2 hospitals, 3 patients, 4 genes, 4 conditions).

You have data from 2 hospitals (batch dim 0).
In each hospital, you study 3 different patients (batch dim 1).
For each patient, you measure 4 genes versus 4 conditions.
That gives you a 4×4 Covariance Matrix

tf.shape(S)[:-2] => We grab the batch part [2, 3]. The first two numbers.
It tells tf.eye to take that 4×4 identity matrix and duplicate it 2 times.

tf.shape(S)[-1] => We grab the matrix size 4. It tells tf.eye to create a
4×4 identity matrix (1s on the diagonal, 0s everywhere else).

Meaning :
The Batched Identity(I), then becomes 2*3(6) copies of the 4×4 identity like below.

Hospital 0 :
Patient 0 → 4×4 matrix
Patient 1 → 4×4 matrix
Patient 2 → 4×4 matrix

Hospital 1 :
Patient 0 → 4×4 matrix
Patient 1 → 4×4 matrix
Patient 2 → 4×4 matrix

Here,
L is a Tool mathematical structure of your past historical data (your model).
Once you calculate it in the morning, you lock it in memory.
You do not change L for the rest of the day.

B is the Specific New Data you want an answer for right now.
B can be Patient_1's lab results. Then B is Patient_2's lab results.
It constantly Changes.
